speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
On Wednesday last, Mr. Speaker, I informed the house of the recommendation conveyed to me by the commissioner of inquiry in the British Columbia coastal shipping strike to the effect that the disputes now at issue between Canadian Pacific Steamships and parties represented by the seafarers international union, the Canadian merchant seamen's guild and the national association of marine engineers be referred to an arbitrator appointed by the Minister of Labour.
On Friday I was able to announce that the recommendation made by Mr. Eric Taylor had been accepted by the Canadian Pacific Railway, by the national association of marine engineers, and by the Canadian merchant seamen's guild. The proposal was rejected by the seafarers international union. Late Friday I therefore invited representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the seafarers international union to meet with me in my office in the labour department to discuss the situation and explore the possibility of finding some ground for mutual agreement.
Present for these talks were Mr. Duncan McNeill, vice president of personnel, and Mr. S. M. Gossage, assistant vice president of personnel for the Canadian Pacific Railway, and Mr. Hal C. Banks and a number of advisers representing the seafarers international union.
I wish to assure the house that all possible avenues of settlement were exhaustively discussed. Unfortunately, however, the parties were unable to agree on a formula for the settlement of the dispute. The government is now taking further steps to reconvene the parties in the dispute for a further meeting in my office within the next few days.

speakerposition: stagedirection

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture based on the concern of farmers' union officials that increased cattle marketings forced by drought conditions may result in a collapse of cattle prices. Has the Manitoba farmers' union requested the minister to fix cattle prices at the level of June 1 in order to prevent a disastrous drop in these prices in Manitoba and other parts of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we received a telegram from Mr. James Patterson, president of the Manitoba farmers' union, a few days ago asking that cattle prices be frozen at the market level of June 1. That, of course, is the highest level at which they have been for some considerable length of time, in fact for several years. I replied stating that there was no power I knew of under any statute of the dominion government by which we could freeze cattle prices at that market level short of proclaiming the War Measures Act, which I think everybody agrees would not be possible, and that therefore this was not a practical or possible solution to the difficulties which the farmers' union was afraid might develop.
I might point out, however, that they also said that a serious weakening of the cattle market was becoming evident and various people have informed us by telegram that there had been a considerable fall in cattle prices. This is not borne out by the figures of cattle prices on the main markets in Canada during the past month. I have a compilation here which I will not read in

full. It indicates what the prices were for the weeks ending June 7, 14, 21, 28 and July 3. During that period good steers have fallen approximately 1 cent a pound at Toronto, from 24.09 cents to 23 cents. At Winnipeg they have fallen from $23.03 a hundred to $22, again approximately a cent a pound. At Calgary they have fallen from $22.40 to $21.60 a hundred or less than a cent a pound.
I might point out also that for the two weeks ending June 28 and July 3 the Chicago price for good steers has increased, the first upward movement there for several weeks prior to that time. Of course, essentially our cattle prices depend upon cattle prices in the United States.
There has been about the same kind of drop in the price of good feeder steers. As a matter of fact, at Winnipeg and Calgary there has been no appreciable drop. At Winnipeg the price was $22.09 on June 7 and it was $22.31 on July 3. Actually, therefore, the prices of feeder steers have gone up at Winnipeg. They are down about half a cent on the Calgary market, and there has been a drop of just under a cent in the price of good cows on all three markets.
This statement to the effect that already there has been a considerable drop in cattle prices as a result of the drought is not borne out by the prices being realized on these various markets. Furthermore yesterday, when I was in Calgary, I talked with a considerable number of cattlemen. They told me there was nothing in that whatever, and they did not anticipate there would be any serious drop in cattle prices.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Can the minister, as a result of his inquiries, assure the house that the packers are not following a policy of downgrading cattle as they come off the pastures, a policy which they frequently follow? My second question is, is it not possible under the agricultural prices stabilization act to set floors above the base price, and a floor at the level of June 1 if the government wished to do so? I think that is a different matter from freezing them.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext:
The request I had, Mr. Speaker, was to freeze those prices at these levels of June 1. So far as setting a support price considerably above the mandatory 80 per cent is concerned, that could be done. However, I do not believe any of the cattlemen in western Canada would approve of it being done. As a matter of fact they are anxious that it not be done, because it would immediately remove our best hope, and our only hope, of getting rid of the surplus cattle we will have. If we put in a support price at that level it would be impossible to export
Inquiries of the Ministry cattle to the United States. We would be cut off from that market. We would have surplus cattle here and would have no place to go with them. In other words we would be cutting our own throats.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext: Is the minister's statement now based on the opinions of the big cattle ranchers or the opinions of the farmers' union which represents the farmers of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRICES BE FIXED AT JUNE 1 LEVEL
speechtext: I disagree.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I was saying I felt certain that the national development program of this government was indeed a political illusion. I recalled that the government did not use the opportunities offered under its national development program during the last session of parliament when immediate expenditures of public moneys would have been very helpful in allaying the serious unemployment problem. As a matter of fact the Prime Minister waited until parliament was prorogued and, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 13, 1958, he kicked off the election campaign with his national development program. In the Ottawa Journal of that date one reads: P.M. Kicks off Campaign
Plans Development Program to provide Jobs for Thousands

Prime Minister Diefenbaker started his election campaign last night with a speech outlining a proposed national development program which he said would make jobs for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
And further down it says:
But the Conservative government had acted with a national program of public works "to provide for the future development of Canada and to assure jobs."
The works program would total $1,185 million of which $270 million would be spent in the first three months of this year.
Although I could use far stronger words than I will use, and I would be quite justified in doing so, I submit that cleverly worded half-truths were deliberately used in order to create the impression in this country that the $1 billion works program was indeed a new plan to put into effect new and economic development projects, and that the spending of the $270 million in the first three months of the year would mean the expenditure of additional money specifically aimed at solving the unemployment problem.
That is not so. The $1,185 million program is, of course, merely part of the ordinary yearly estimated governmental expenditure-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but I must ask that members in all parts of the house moderate their conversation so we can hear the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres.

This amount of $1,185 million constitutes part of the ordinary yearly estimated amount which governments have spent over the years, and as a matter of fact it is only some $34 million more than was spent in the previous fiscal year. Furthermore, the $270 million which was supposed to have been spent in the first three months of the year is the normal amount of money which a government would spend in the first quarter of any fiscal year, and I certainly hope that no one is trying to explain or write off the $1 billion deficit by the existence of a new public works and national development program because, of course, there is no such new development program.
I respectfully submit that this practice of using half-truths and subterfuges in some of the official statements which are made is a very dangerous policy which undermines the very existence of our democratic system. The people of Canada cannot possibly be abreast of all the administrative details of government, and as a matter of fact they have no alternative but to have faith in the words of our political leaders. I say that it is not only an undemocratic but it is an intolerably iniquitous and dangerous practice for the government by a shrewd juggling of figures
National Development Policy and words to make the people of Canada believe something which is not in accordance with the facts.
The sum of $1,185 million for a national development program as tabled in the estimates and supplementary estimates for 195859 can be divided up in this way. For public works we find expenditures, including the erection and maintenance of public buildings such as post offices and other buildings, and construction and maintenance of wharves, docks, bridges and roads in national parks, amounting to some $145 million. Expenditures for the Department of Transport include such items as construction and maintenance of airports, some work for the Department of National Defence, the national harbours board and construction and maintenance of deep-sea piers, wharves and grain elevators at major ports and expenditures for the St. Lawrence seaway and Trans-Canada Airlines totalling $244 million.
Last night the Minister of Transport in an intervention, told the house that this government had spent more than twice the amount spent by the previous Liberal government; yet according to the estimates and the sup-plementaries the department plans to spend $260 million. Last year $220 million were spent by that department, which makes a difference of $40 million, which is a far cry from being more than double the amount spent by the previous government.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I should like to correct the hon. member, as I am sure he would like to have the facts straight. What I said last night was that as far as steamship construction was concerned we were spending $22 million this year as against $9 million spent by the Liberal government as recorded in the estimates of last year, and that as far as airport construction is concerned our estimates this year are nearly double.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I did not say that the Department of Transport over-all was spending twice what the department had spent a year ago.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is certainly no question of privilege in that-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The hon. member merely deliberately misquoted me; that is the only question of privilege.

-nevertheless I am happy that the Minister of Transport saw fit to make that statement. I was eager to ensure that the impression was not created in the public mind that this department is spending twice as much this year as was spent last year under the Liberal administration.

National Development Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman would
listen and pay attention to what was being said he would not be under a misapprehension.

To continue the discussion of the estimates, the expenditures for defence include expected construction and maintenance expenditures by the Department of National Defence itself and Defence Construction Limited totalling $80 million. The expenditures for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation include expected expenditures on construction and maintenance of public housing units including some buildings for the Department of National Defence and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans totalling $308 million. The items for the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources include expected expenditures on projects in the farthest northern parts of Canada, including those of the northern Canada power commission, the development of thermal power units in the Atlantic provinces and construction in the national parks totalling $50 million. The items for crown corporations include expected expenditures connected with construction and maintenance by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the northern Ontario pipe line, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Canadian Arsenals and Polymer Corporation totalling $72 million. For the Canadian National Railways there are items covering expected expenditures on construction and maintenance during the calendar year 1958 totalling $140 million.
Federal financial support to other works projects include works projects carried out co-operatively with provincial and municipal governments which are not included under items of federal support such as the trans-Canada highway, hospital construction, railway grade crossings, technical schools and other expenditures totalling $100 million. Other departments and agencies include the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Justice, the federal district commission, the South Saskatchewan project and others totalling $46 million. The particular item for the South Saskatchewan project is shown as $8 million. That is about the only new project that is included in the estimates; of course we know it has not been started as yet and indeed there seem to be some difficulties which must be overcome before it can be commenced.
When the hon. member for Essex East asked the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources when he was explaining his northern projects how much had been included for them in the estimates, the minister did not immediately answer. It was only after a considerable length of time that

we learned that there was an amount of $3.8 million for surveys and an additional $50,000 for research included in the minister's departmental estimates of $50 million. This breakdown of the $1,185 million for new development projects differs greatly from the story that appeared in the Ottawa Journal on February 13, 1958. In that article we read:
Mr. Diefenbaker emphasized the north as he talked about Canadian development. He mentioned his hopes for a "self-governing north".
Under the development plan would come:
1.	Arctic research and exploration of the Arctic archipelago aimed at developing resources that Canadians little realized.
2.	A $100 million roads program in the Yukon and Northwest Territories to allow exploration of new mineral areas.
3.	A federal-provincial plan to build access roads to the north, tying in with roads in the Territories. It would cost $75 million and perhaps twice that if all provinces joined.
4.	Aid to economically sound railway projects, such as the proposed line from northern Alberta to Pine Point on Great Slave lake.
5.	A $75 million development at the northern community of Frobisher Bay on Baffin island.
The program would mean jobs for "hundreds of thousands of Canadians" and would open the way for investment "by Canadian and foreign investors of hundreds of millions of dollars".
Let me hasten to state that the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are still without work and who had hopes of being able to find employment in the north are doomed to bitter disappointment because, as a matter of fact, not one of those items is included in the estimates the government has brought forward this year. May I also point out that even if these huge sums had been included in the estimates an obvious question arises. Where is the economic logic of opening new resources in the north at this time when we cannot find sufficient outlets for similar resources that are at hand and which we have as yet hardly tapped? Why should the government spend hundreds of millions of dollars in the construction of roads leading to resources that are as yet undiscovered, when private enterprise and private investment capital are not as yet even exploiting the newly-found resources they have at hand?
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources yesterday bandied about hundreds of millions of dollars. He mentioned of course, that those were sums that private investors and private capital would invest. However, he did not give any authoritative source for the figures which he placed on the record. He did not say whether these represented binding commitments on the part of specific corporations. He mentioned vaguely letters of intent without, of course, referring to the date of these letters of intent. Need I point out that something that might have been economically sound three years ago may

not necessarily be economically sound at the present time under existing economic conditions.
To my mind the majority of the provinces are already overburdened with more pressing and more vital commitments at this time and simply cannot afford to engage capital in such long-range projects as proposed by the minister of northern affairs. There will come a time when economic and social conditions in Canada as well as in the provinces will not only warrant but will necessitate such expenditures, but to my way of thinking we have not yet arrived at that day; and any serious attempt to make the northern vision come true at this time would indeed be trying to run before we can walk.
There are too many lacunas in our economic and social set-up and too many urgent economic development projects of all types to be realized in the inhabited area of our country to embark on a huge building program in the uninhabited area for resources for which there seems to be no urgent need at this time, and which we might well leave to those generations of Canadians yet unborn who may have a far greater need for them than we have. Any attempt now to make the Prime Minister's vision of a self-governing north come true would be taking a bite out of a huge piece of responsibility without having half digested that very heavy responsibility which the government has to face at the present time.
There are hundreds of segments of our economy in the immediate area which are in urgent need of projects which come within the jurisdiction of the federal government, and which I claim might more easily provide work for the hundreds of thousands of people who are still unemployed in our country. There are bridges; there are tunnels, causeways, underpasses, railroads, airports, port facilities, which are urgently required from one end of our country to the other and which I am sure would contribute greatly to the economic growth and stabilization of our country.
There is, of course, another great economic problem that arises out of the relationship of the federal and the provincial governments, and more particularly the municipal governments. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not forgotten about the municipal problem. At page 29 of Hansard of January 9, 1957, the Prime Minister had this to say:
There are many things with which we agree. We agree-
He was speaking of Mr. Harris' budget.
-as to the need for assistance to the municipalities across this country.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in the budget that has anything to do with the
National Development Policy municipalities. There is nothing either in the vision or in the government's national development program that may be construed as assistance to municipalities. There is a vague promise of holding a federal-provincial-municipal conference at an indeterminate time and also with an undetermined agenda. I submit that is not assistance; that is merely procrastination.
I certainly hope the conference will take place soon and that concrete solutions will be found to the inter-governmental fiscal policy; but surely, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, with all the experience he has had and with the innumerable briefs that have been submitted to him on this problem, is aware that apart from this very difficult fiscal problem the municipalities are confronted with a multitude of problems for which government assistance could and should have been provided under a national development program.
The government national development program might have given special attention to the construction of projects coming within its jurisdiction which would have been of particular economic value to the municipalities. I do not know all the projects that might be useful to municipalities, but I do know of one in my own riding, where the project would be not only of national value but of extreme help to the municipalities in one whole area. I am referring to Sorel, which is a port on the St. Lawrence seaway about 50 miles below Montreal, at the junction of the Richelieu river which, as hon. members know, is a direct water route to New York by way of lake Champlain.
Ever since before confederation this route has been used for trade by small boats, and we had always heard and read about the project for an internal waterway in that area. It was only in 1938 that the then member for Richelieu-Vercheres, the late Hon. Mr. Cardin, actually started the project by having the Richelieu river dredged to 12 feet in several of its areas, with a dam at St. Ours and Fryar island to enable ships with a draft of 12 to 14 feet to go through.
The war came along and the project had to be stopped. Since then the Richelieu river has become a forgotten waterway. Yet, in spite of very difficult conditions, where the river is only six feet in depth in certain sections, and in spite of the interminable dams and locks at St. Johns, this river has been used in the past for a considerable amount of trade. I would like to pay tribute here to what I believe to be one of the pioneers of this new water route, the Guy Tombs Company Limited, which under very serious difficulties has continued over the years to have a fleet of ships travelling along that particular waterway.

National Development Policy
The United States is equally interested in realizing this waterway, and recently when a delegation from my riding presented a brief to the Prime Minister concerning this project there were indications that representatives from the United States were willing to effect their part of the work on the Hudson river, to realize an international waterway of a depth of 12 feet. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that with the industrialization that has taken place below Sorel this would be an economically sound project.
I would also say this. Since Canada is now engaged with the United States in the joint defence of the North American continent, I submit that it would be extremely useful to have an inland water route to New York by way of the Richelieu river and the Hudson river. This project would not only bring more into the Canadian economy and national security than it would take out of it from a national point of view, but it would also, I believe, be of tremendous assistance to a countless number of municipalities along the Richelieu river.
This is but one example, Mr. Speaker, of a national development project which would be useful to the national economy and which would at the same time be of tremendous help to the municipalities. Another municipal problem, apart from the taxation problem and apart from their insufficient revenue potential, is that practically all municipalities have arrived at the point in their evolution when serious attention should be given to the elimination of blighted and substandard areas that exist, unfortunately, in most municipalities and which are not in keeping with the economic and social development that has taken place in recent years. It seems to me that before trying to conquer new fields, a national development program should be helping our municipalities to get rid of those dwellings that are not only veritable firetraps but are completely incompatible with the moral and physical health standards that we have a right to expect in a country like Canada.
A well balanced national development policy should include an urban redevelopment program such as the Liberal party and my leader advocated yesterday under which, because of the staggering costs of acquiring and clearing substandard areas, the federal government should bring in an amendment to the legislation which was introduced by the previous government so that the federal government would assume 75 per cent instead of 50 per cent of the cost of acquiring substandard areas, and also to furnish additional help to the municipalities by sharing the cost of water, sewers and other municipal services.

Apart from this program there is another serious and urgent problem facing municipalities, namely the problem of providing municipal facilities and community growth requirements which alone impose such financial burdens on the municipalities that they have to have recourse to means other than taxation to meet their obligations. They are forced to borrow money at rates which in most cases are prohibitive. The Prime Minister is well aware of this problem because on March 28, 1957-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It might be interesting to read what the Prime Minister had to say on this problem as found at page 2777 of Hansard for March 28, 1957. He said:
Cities across the nation find themselves actually in a position where the costs of borrowing are making it impossible for them to carry on the ordinary and requisite expenditures to meet an ever-increasing population. What is the government going to do about it? What action does the government intend to take? It superintended the imposition of higher interest rates. It refuses to reduce its wasteful expenditure. It refuses, as I said a moment ago, to permit the setting up of either a commission or committees to recommend
National Development Policy
action. All of us agree with the objective, namely, that this situation must be met. The only difference between us is that we do not believe it can be met with a government that persists in spending and increasing its expenditures without regard to the effects of these increases.
I recall very well, Mr. Speaker, all the eloquence and finger shaking that accompanied the Prime Minister's words pronounced just a little over a year ago. But when we examine at length the billion dollar deficit, and when we realize that in spite of all the very fine oratory no mention was made of the municipalities' difficulties in borrowing money in the Prime Minister's national development program or elsewhere, we can very well wonder whether the Prime Minister is not placing much too much emphasis on oratory and not sufficient emphasis on logic.
The Prime Minister, of course, might have done a great deal worse than take the suggestion made by my leader yesterday of creating a municipal loan fund in order to make additional money available to municipalities at a reasonably low cost. This, I submit, would not only have provided money to permit municipalities to engage in necessary municipal projects, but also would have enabled them to provide work for the countless numbers of unemployed now plaguing each municipality. Certainly legislation along this line would not only have assisted municipalities in facing up to their increasing responsibilities but would have been an effective part of a practical, if not of a visionary, national development program.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with mixed feelings. I am happy that I am given the opportunity to perhaps educate some of the hon. members opposite as to what is actually going on in parts of the northern territories of Canada. It rather made me a little sad while I was listening to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) to think that he thought we in the Yukon and Northwest Territories are something less than Canadians.
I never said that.

The hon. member for
Richelieu-Vercheres stated in his remarks that these areas are uninhabited. I can assure him that they are inhabited, and I will have more to say about the remarks of some other hon. members of the Liberal party in that regard later. There are people there. These people are Canadians and they are proud of that fact. These people are pioneers. In some cases they have been there for 60 years waiting for someone with a little aggressiveness and gumption to come along and do something about developing the country.

National Development Policy All through the debate on the speech from the throne various hon. members opposite rose and ridiculed the vision we have been speaking about, not just in the weeks leading up to the last election but for years. They have ridiculed it as electioneering. They have reviled it out of jealousy that they did not have the foresight to plan it before this aggressive group did. They have scorned it as unimportant compared with other areas of Canada. They have scoffed at it so as to belittle its true importance to unity and to the necessity for national development. They have dismissed it as some sort of illusion or mirage. All these terms have been used.
But all along these same people who have used these terms have claimed the credit for the plans that are now being put into effect in the northern regions of Canada. They have claimed credit for these plans because they thought it was of some benefit to them to do so. Despite all this invective coming from the opposite benches they claim these plans as Liberal, as something good, so why do we have all the criticism? If the plans are good, and they must be good if they claim them as Liberal, then why do we have all the criticism?
I thought I might, for the benefit of some of the members, do a little take-off on the poems of Robert Service. I have four such compositions for which I should like to ask your forbearance. One of these I have composed concerns the lack of Liberal policy in the north, and it is a take-off on "Sam McGee", with apologies to Robert Service:
There was lots undone in the midnight sun By the government of old
The people up there had heard great tales- For twenty-two years they were told!
The northern lights have seen queer sights But the queerest they ever did see Was June the tenth-the reckonin' day Still no Liberal policy!
Now this great land for so many years Had heard these promises all And the trusting souls who lived up there Thought the Liberals on the ball But nary a plan was ever in sight Mapping northern development 'Til the P.C.'s came along one day And formed the government.
There are now things done in the midnight sun By the men who have the power Soon Arctic trails will tell their tales Of Yukon's finest hour.
For a national policy just can be We differ from Mr. Lesage And Lionel, there are others up there Excluding poor Sam on Lebarge.
Bold and fearless, sound and strong,
Must be our policy Impossible said Minister Lesage And Liberals all agreed.
Those in the north, they're just not there Said Mr. Chevrier too
But the biggest mistake that was made by far Was Mike's famed igloo.

Let me return to serious discussion for a moment and see what the policy was, or lack of policy, under the former administration. I refer to Hansard for February 12, 1957, page 1197-

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order. Yesterday the leader of the house took exception to discussions of a retrospective character in this debate. He said that the motion dealt with the future and not with the past. It seems to me I shall have his full support in raising the question as to whether or not these discussions about the past have anything to do with the motion before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
