speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On the contrary, it was willingly accepted.

The former minister,
Mr. Lesage, had this to say at page 1197 of Hansard for February 12, 1957:
Therefore, it is really since the post-war period that it has been possible to look forward to our northern development.
He further said that most of the development was made possible after the Liberal administration had been relieved of the pressures generated by the second world war. On page 1198 he went on to say:
Then there is the human problem of this population in the north. We cannot develop 40 per cent of Canada in five years-

No one has any quarrel with him there.
-I do not believe we can have people who are still living in the stone age transferred overnight to the atomic age.
Apparently this statement is along the same lines as the thinking of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. I should like to reiterate that we are not in the stone age in the Yukon. I am happy to see that the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie) has just entered the chamber. I am sorry he was not here while the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres was speaking, because I am sure he would have been disappointed to hear a member of his party advocate the position his party takes with respect to the north.
Then on page 1199 of Hansard, to which I have referred, Mr. Lesage said:
So the Leader of the Opposition wishes to have a national plan-an over-all master plan for the development and management of resources in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it is up to the federal government to initiate, produce and administer such a national policy according to such a master plan.
We see here, clearly elucidated in the statement by the minister of northern affairs in the last administration, that a national development plan is impossible. Time after time the present Prime Minister has referred to the need for a national development policy. A brief sketch of the history of the proposals put forward from time to time when this party was in opposition is contained in a speech made by the present Prime Minister on February 11, 1957, commencing on page 1153 of Hansard. The Prime Minister went briefly over the history from the most recent representations back to June 16, 1952, when certain amendments were recorded containing statements connecting this party with definite policies.
At that time also the Gordon commission was discussed. The Prime Minister had this to say about it:
There has been a thunderous silence on the part of the government with respect to the action that it intends to take in this regard.
The reference is to the various proposals put forward by the Gordon commission with respect to national development and development of the north. It is only now that the Liberal party has come forward with anything concrete in the way of a national development policy, and that is in the form of this amendment. We have the former minister's statement that there can be no such national plan, yet we have the anomaly of this amendment which, incidentally, is being supported by the C.C.F. group and which is directly contrary to the policy expressed by the previous minister.
National Development Policy
I might say that that announcement of policy was made by the former minister during the throne speech debate during February of 1957, and the amendment was put forward by the present Prime Minister. This amendment, calling for a national development plan, was supported by the C.C.F. group. I realize that it is not proper to comment on the way in which any particular member of the house voted, but I may say here that at that time the amendment proposed by the Prime Minister was defeated by a vote of 121 to 67, the C.C.F. group voting as a whole with us.
We have also heard from the Leader of the Opposition and from the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres that the truth is, if the truth were known, that these plans concerning the north were not our plans at all but were the policies of the former government. I wonder whether they were the policies of the former government. Inasmuch as statements of the facts are not a monopoly of hon. members opposite, perhaps we might put some facts on the record as well.
I am now going to quote from a speech made by the hon. member who had the honour to represent the riding of Yukon in 1957 and who, as is obvious, was subsequently defeated. Perhaps this quotation which I am about to read will give an explanation why. I have spoken about the ridicule which has been heaped upon this idea of a vision of northern development. Let me read from the speech by Mr. Simmons on January 15, 1957, as reported at page 264 of Hansard of that date:
Just at this point I might say that the previous financial agreement between the federal government and the territorial government will expire on March 31 of this year. A new agreement will then come into effect. The agreement presently in force has most certainly failed to meet the present needs of this fast-developing territory because of the shortsighted, penny-pinching attitude of those people in the department who formulated the policy contained in the agreement when it was drawn up about five years ago. It is to be hoped that improved vision and better understanding will be displayed in connection with the drafting of the new fiscal arrangements.
That was a member of the Liberal party speaking about his own government of the day and their approach to northern development. He went on to say this with regard to the outlook for the north:
I have no doubt that the persistence which these oil explorers are known to possess, their skill and the money which they are willing to venture will lead to the discovery of further oil fields in this area.
Speaking about this risk capital, which the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources spoke about yesterday and which the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres has

National Development Policy dismissed as figures which are being bandied about, may I remind hon. members opposite that the hon. member for Essex East has said that Right Hon. Mr. Howe, when he was in this house, said that this was a possible estimate as far back as three years ago.
Three years ago there was a boom.

Hence when the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres makes statements to the effect that there are half truths and subterfuge, and when he perhaps accuses this party of creating misconceptions in the public mind, if I were that hon. member I would have regard to these facts.
Further as to this vision, and going back to Mr. Simmons, as reported at page 266 of Hansard, in speaking of the road program we find him saying this:
The road would be one of the most important projects that could be undertaken to promote the economic welfare and stability of .the northern Mackenzie river district,-
He is speaking of the self-same road that has received so much criticism, the one going through to the vicinity of Fort McPherson.
-as well as the northern Yukon areas. In fact it would be nothing less than culpable neglect on the part of the government to sidestep further this highly significant and very practical measure.
This is Mr. Simmons speaking, a member of the Liberal party.
If our north country is to be opened and developed in the way it should be, the federal government should assist the companies and individuals who are willing to risk capital in such ventures, especially in areas which are favourable to mineral development... .Development of its mineral resources has been retarded throughout the years by the lack of roads, the result of a lack of administrative vision__
The arrangement with the federal government on the Canol road-
About which I will have further remarks to make later.
-promised a maximum of $2,500 a year for maintenance, provided the company expended $2,500 a year. When it is considered that this sum was to provide for the maintenance of 150 miles of gravel road, including 21 timber bridges and 40 culverts,
it can be seen how niggardly this assistance is__
The indifference of those responsible for the maintenance of this asset is difficult to understand_
As far as is known, no maintenance has been provided by the federal or territorial governments during that time with the exception of the paltry sum I have previously mentioned.
Then at page 268 we find this:
Official thinking here in Ottawa has in the past fallen far short of meeting the real problem. There has not been the necessary vision on the part of officials to grasp the requirements of the situation.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the previous Liberal member for Yukon expounding what have

long been Conservative policies. Perhaps that is the reason for his acute criticism of the lack of action on the part of his colleagues who formed the last government.
As to national development and the national development policy itself may I say this. The Leader of the Opposition says that national development should not merely be centred on northern development. Again I would draw the hon. member's attention to the speech that was made by the Prime Minister as reported in Hansard of 1957, where over and over again he stressed the fact that a national development policy must have regard to a co-operative program of development entered into with the provinces and the territories. Hence it is wrong to create the illusion that this party is attempting to centre national development policy on Canada's north. Our policy is not centred on the northland. Certainly there is an emphasis which is being given to northern development, but there is not a centring there of all national development. One has only to look at such projects as the Beechwood project, the South Saskatchewan river dam and others that are in the making.
The Leader of the Opposition also stated that we should have a balanced policy. I do not mean to offer criticism of the Leader of the Opposition simply for the sake of criticism, but I say this. Even if it cannot be said, "Why didn't you do it", certainly one cannot stand idly by and hear a brand new policy being expounded by the Leader of the Opposition without drawing attention to the glaring fact that if this amendment which is now before the house constitutes a policy, it is the first time that any policy of national development has been expounded by anyone in the Liberal party.

I am sure the hon. member wiU want to be very fair in his observation. The Leader of the Opposition expounded a policy which was predicated in part upon the decline in public investment in Canada at the present time, which is quite a different situation.

I was coming to that in a moment, and I was only making the point that the Leader of the Opposition did go so far as to say that there was now a change in the economic situation and that therefore we must have a flexible national development policy. That, indeed, is true, and I concede that much to the hon. member for Essex East; but I think he must agree with me that this is still the first time that any national development policy, as such, has been expounded by any member of the Liberal party.

The Leader of the Opposition gave a short review of what the policy had been in the past, and he spoke of the great advance in the development of the north immediately after the second world war. He spoke of housing and forest inventories, reforestation and fire prevention and all the grants therefor. Again I do not know whether a series of such accomplishments can be lumped together and called a policy. I do not believe so but I believe we can have a firm national development policy such as that expounded on February 12 by the present Prime Minister, and as recounted in the house yesterday by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources; firm but flexible. Indeed, I do believe that the program set forth by the minister is flexible enough to cope with any economic fluctuations which may occur in the national economy.
I only have to think of the possibility of the projected development at Coppermine, which I believe is what the Leader of the Opposition had in mind. When the economic situation develops to a point which would warrant such development a road will be extended to that area. That is the way the minister explained it; and when one speaks of a national development policy and national housing development I can only say that until this government came along there were, I believe, three units constructed under the National Housing Act in the whole of the Yukon territory. One can see how marvellously that legislation worked out in the Yukon. There are changes in sight which will enable low rental housing schemes to be put into effect, and in fact one such scheme has been authorized very recently by the present government and undoubtedly it will be implemented in the very near future.
The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres have both said that these plans are not new, and the hon. member for Mackenzie River interjected during the speech of the minister attributing certain advances in the north to the previous administration. At that time I wondered where was the Liberal plan for the Flat creek to Fort McPherson road; where was the plan of the previous administration for that road? Where was the plan for the construction of the bridge over the Yukon river at Carmacks? Where was the plan for the construction of the Pelly river bridge? Where was the plan for the construction of a bridge over the Stewart river, and where was the plan for the construction of the Flat creek road into Dawson by Rock Creek Bluffs? Where was the plan for the new schools which are going to be built in the
National Development Policy Yukon and where was the plan for the airport improvements which will be going forward up there? Where was the plan of the last administration for the improvement of the Elsa road and where was the plan for the improvement of the Dawson-Stewart road and the Tatchun creek bridge? The hon. member for Mackenzie River was holding up a map a moment ago; were these plans mere lines on a map?
I am looking at the report of the commissioner of the Yukon Territory to the Gordon commission.

Where is this declared policy of the previous government? Where is the declared policy of the Liberal government to actively put these projects into effect? I defy any Liberal member to say that these projects had been planned actively by the past administration.
The Stewart-Cassiar road, did you say?

No, I did not. I mentioned the Flat creek to Fort McPherson road, the bridge at Carmacks, the Pelly river bridge, the Stewart river bridge, the Flat creek road to Dawson, the schools, the airports, the improvement of the Elsa road, the Dawson-Stewart road and the Tatchun creek bridge. I might add that the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources have been increased by 400 per cent this year. These estimates have been increased by this government and not by the previous administration; and if these plans are Liberal plans, why did they not appear in the previous administration's estimates? Again I challenge any one of the Liberal members to show me the estimates where these projects are shown.
I would now like to read from Saturday Night of January 19, 1957, as follows: Northerners stress that the mineral resources of this vast hinterland should not be measured by the mines and prospects that have already been found, but by the geology of the region. Roughly a third of the Canadian shield, the area in which are located the Sudbury, Timmins and Noranda deposits, lies in the Territories-
And, northerners add, they are hampered by an outdated government policy. They charge government officials still are trying to make work the "rule of thumb" used 25 or 30 years ago.
"People on the outside look on the north as a romantic country developed by the government," said Norman Byrne, a mining consultant and veteran of 20 years in the north. "But what has the government done to develop the country? All the development here has been by private enterprise and not the government. Their policy seems to be 'You spend the money opening up the country, and then we'll think about helping you or paying you back'-just the opposite to the point of view the government should have."

National Development Policy And that point of view is held by this government.
Mr. Byrne charged the government seems to think mining is a promotion which doesn't always pay for itself. "The government seems to base its thinking-''
He is here speaking of the Liberal government of the day, of course.
"-on the premise that a mine must have a 10 or 20 year supply of ore in sight before it does anything to help the industry. The current thinking of leading mining men is that if a company has three or four years in sight, it is justified in bringing a property into production if production will pay for the gamble and provide a return on the money invested."
He stressed mining companies need help when they are struggling to get into production, when it is difficult to get the needed finances.
I would just like to make one comment while on this article in Saturday Night about the total lack of foresight and lack of policy on the part of the previous administration. During the war, a road and a pipe line were constructed up there, namely from Johnson's Crossing in Yukon Territory to Norman Wells. This road was constructed at a cost of roughly $500 million, and it was given to Canada at the end of the war. On this subject Saturday Night has this to say:
An example, now almost forgotten, is the construction of the Canol pipe line and road to carry Norman Wells oil to a refinery at Whitehorse, Yukon, during the second world war. Roughly half a billion dollars were poured into the mammoth task of pushing the line and road over the sawtooth Mackenzie mountains and across the muskeg and turbulent rivers.
When the war ended, the refinery was dismantled and shipped to Edmonton. Before the bridges were washed away and the roadbed crumbled, crews salvaged as much of the abandoned equipment and pipe as possible and disposed of it at distress prices. All that remains of this defence effort is an impassable road along which is strewn some obsolete and worthless equipment.
I am very happy to say that this road will be rehabilitated this year. In all fairness to the previous administration, they did plan to do this work and laid out about one-third of the money necessary for this purpose. They planned a visionary, active and aggressive three-year program for rehabilitation of this kind while there were ore beds in the territory awaiting development. It will be done in one year. This is a perfect example of the so-called planning that was conducted under the previous administration.
I promised the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) that I would deal with what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said yesterday. At page 1963 of yesterday's Hansard the Leader of the Opposition is reported as having said:
-our post-war development of this country was tempered by our desire in those years to postpone 
what could be reasonably postponed so It would not compete with the high level of private investment.
He went on to say:
I do not for one minute, however, accept the contention of Conservative spokesmen in the last election campaign that this kind of program in the Arctic about which they talked at that time, a road program, a transportation program, would have any considerable effect, if any effect at all, in the immediate emergency which confronted us, which was unemployment. It is one thing to put forward a program for national development in the Arctic,-
That is stretching the truth of the program, in effect.
-but it is another thing to put forward a program of that kind especially when it is contained in estimates which already have been drawn up as a cure for the unemployment emergency.
I submit that this argument is fallacious. In attempting to explain away the reason why the Liberal party did not have a policy the Leader of the Opposition said that it was the desire of the Liberal administration- to quote the hon. gentleman's words:
-to postpone what could be reasonably postponed so it would not compete with the high level of private investment.
We can see how false that argument is because by not postponing the construction of the Flat Creek-Aklavik road we now have an investment of between $150 million and $250 million of private money being pumped into our economy.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he tell us when this sum of between $150 million and $200 million will be spent?

If the hon. member for Mackenzie River had been here throughout the entire course of the speech made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) yesterday, he would have the answer to his question.
There was no answer to that question.

I might mention that I cannot understand the hon. member for Mackenzie River having the temerity to criticize this program, coming as he does from an area of Canada which is so very much in need of the type of development for which this program provides.
I asked you a question, my boy.

I must also admit that I cannot understand either why hon. members of the C.C.F. group would support the motion they did during the throne speech debate on the last occasion on which the Liberal administration brought down a throne speech because in essence it was opposed to what they are supporting today.
Not at all.

It is on the record and you have only to read it. This political flexibility of the Liberal and C.C.F. parties has always amazed me. I sometimes like to refer to it not as a schizophrenic split personality but as a split morality.
The Leader of the Opposition also dealt with the national development program which was first expounded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on February 12, and as reported at page 1963 of yesterday's Hansard the Leader of the Opposition said:
This kind of claim during an election campaign or subsequent to an election campaign, and even if it is made in this house this afternoon, does not make sense. A program of national development in the north to improve transportation and communication for national development purposes, carrying on the planning and development which has been going on for years, does make sense.
"A program of national development in the north," was not what was said by either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. They and other hon. members in this party have all along referred to a truly national development plan involving the co-operation of the provinces and the territories. Again I remind hon. gentlemen in all parts of the house and members of the public generally that the national development program of this government is not confined to the north.
One has only to look at the figures to realize how much development has been going on in years past. The expenditures by the previous administration in the construction of new Yukon roads in 1944-45 were $20,500; in 1955-56, $152,500; and in 1956-57, $75,000. The estimates for this year for the construction of roads in the Yukon territory total $452,000. The estimates of the previous administration for the last fiscal year for the construction of roads and bridges in the Yukon territory amounted to $480,941. The estimates for this year represent an expenditure of $3,138,600.
While time still permits I wish to refer to a pamphlet published by the national Liberal federation for use in the last election campaign entitled ''For Jobs, for Peace, Vote the Pearson Plan". I have read it from cover to cover and it contains this interesting statement:
Northern Development-A long-term program of northern development including prompt construction of a railroad to Great Slave lake.
This is the national development policy which was expounded afresh by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday? I thought perhaps hon. members opposite would eventually come to believe that the north represented an area worthwhile of development but on
National Development Policy the basis of the statements they have made I am disappointed. Perhaps I should not have been disappointed in view of an article which appeared in the London Free Press on February 18,	1958 under the headline,
"Charges 'Panic' of PC's Forced Winter Election." The article reports on a speech made by the Leader of the Opposition on an occasion when he shared the platform with the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). The article reads in part as follows:
Joining him on the program was Lionel Chevrier, one-time transport minister and the federal Liberal party's top man in Quebec.
Mr. Chevrier suggested the party's election pledge of $400 million in tax cuts was a far better solution to unemployment problems than the Conservatives' national works program.
Unemployment was found in heavily-populated areas, such as Quebec. But the Conservatives were planning construction in far-off places, such as a $100 million highway in the Yukon vicinity "where there is nobody__and therefore no unemployment."
"Do the Conservatives intend to force the unemployed of our cities to leave for the far north of our country to find jobs?" he asked.
His remarks imply that the hon. member for Laurier does not feel that this is the way the people are thinking. We have already heard a great deal about the "igloo to igloo" statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I must advise him that his time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, there was some time taken up in discussing a point of order while I was speaking and I wonder if I have been given credit for that time?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Actually I was out of the chair so I cannot say. I am told that you already have had two minutes additional time. However, if you confine your remarks to a minimum and if it is the pleasure of the house to permit the hon. member to carry on I suppose this would be all right.
I have just three or four minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to permit the hon. member for the Yukon to continue?
Yes.

Thank you. I just have one word left concerning the demand for minerals, and I refer to an article in the U.S. News and World Report in support of the proposition of ours that as the demand is increasing, it is not wise to wait for the maximum development of that demand before this government starts to think about development roads. We have to keep ahead of the game. We cannot start building the roads when the demand is there; we have to anticipate the

National Development Policy demand. This is only prudent. This article in the U.S. News and World Report, a United States publication, describes the area of northern Canada and it goes on to say that:
United States planners heave a sigh of relief when they look at Canada's northwest.
In that great wilderness is a treasure trove of oil, nickel, copper, uranium and a host of other minerals that the United States needs in ever increasing quantities.
I quote this, Mr. Speaker, because we must look not only to the development of our resources for all Canadians in all parts of Canada but we must anticipate the demand and we must anticipate it in such a way that we shall maintain for Canadians now and in the future our economic sovereignty over the host of minerals that will be developed as a result of this program.
I close on this note, Mr. Speaker. We, in the Yukon at any rate, have long awaited the aggressiveness and the farsighted and visionary policies that this government is now putting forward and certainly the Yukon as well as the Northwest Territories, is just waiting to spill those riches into the lap of the waiting world. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, after having listened to the speeches of hon. members of the opposition so far in this debate, that we in the north can thank our lucky stars and the intelligent exercise of the franchise by the Canadian electorate on March 31 when they decided to accept the development policy of the present government, without which we would still be languishing, and I am sure in the future we would maintain, our position as a second-rate mineral producer. Thank you.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to support the amendment proposed by my leader. In spite of expansion there seems to be a tendency to tighten and to restrict trade. This seems to be the appropriate time to get on with some of those works and needed facilities which could not be done during the golden age of Liberal prosperity because people we re busy doing other things; but I would like to speak particularly on transportation and specifically at the moment on the trans-Canada highway in the Atlantic provinces.
Even with the 50-50 formula, the building of the trans-Canada highway places very heavy burdens on the Atlantic provinces. The -90-10 support policy was not sufficient to relieve the pressure of this burden. My leader promised that if elected he would build 90 per cent of the mileage of the roads through the Atlantic provinces. I would like to request that if the government cannot see its way to carry out that policy, it at least consider giving additional help. In my own

province of Newfoundland I would suggest that perhaps if the government would take over a hundred miles of the trans-Canada highway, that is an additional 100 miles, it would give a great deal of aid which would be of great value in completing a very badly needed facility. It would aid in the speeding up of the building of the trans-Canada highway from coast to coast and would permit the provincial government to give more attention to roads leading to the smaller and more remote settlements where road transportation facilities are badly needed.
In addition to the trans-Canada highway as it is now, I would like to suggest that a road leading from Grand Falls up the great northern peninsula be built and considered as a part of the trans-Canada highway and that some means of transportation across the strait of Belle Isle might be considered. Perhaps the most feasible would be a ferry on the strait but the possibilities of a causeway, which has already been mentioned, or of tunnelling under the strait, should not be overlooked. I know that in . the future direct road communications between the island of Newfoundland and the mainland would be of great value.
In addition to roadbuilding in the island itself, there is strong reason to believe that a road built up the coast of Labrador would be very desirable. Perhaps for more immediate consideration we should think of air strips in Labrador. The forerunner of development is the float plane. After the float plane come the larger land planes which are required to bring in equipment needed to develop natural resources, and that indicates airstrips. Airstrips could very well be the forerunners of the roads to resources, the roads to development of the north, and I must admit I am particularly interested in the Labrador which, in a big way is my part of the north. It is also probably the oldest part of the north as far as our nation of Canada goes.
Then the matter of highways to supplement coastal services should be considered. This is not a new idea but I do hope that the idea, although it germinated during Liberal days, will not be overlooked. At the present time, at enormous cost, coastal steamers are built and operated, giving water transportation which has been traditional in Newfoundland for many years; but as roads begin to finger up the various and more remote parts of the island people are more and more desirous of having road communication. It is faster and more practical. Mail delivered by roads gets there faster than by boat, and I am not so sure that roads are more expensive than steamers. I would respectfully ask the government to consider the possibility of

using highroads to supplement at least in part coastal services by steamer.
Again, in connection with transportation, I would like to mention the harbour development in St. John's. My reason for mentioning this is that the schooner operators from White bay and Green bay are just as much interested in what happens in St. John's harbour as the people of St. John's themselves or anyone else.
Everyone seems to have a different opinion as to what should be done at St. John's and I suppose it requires a certain amount of temerity to mention the subject. But I am convinced that the plan prepared by the Department of Public Works is not only a good one but the correct one. There is only one possible criticism I can see, that it does not extend around the harbour far enough. But that is scarcely a criticism because if time and circumstance should make it desirable to extend it there is nothing to stop extension of work already done. Even the criticism that the wharf commonly called the Finger wharf, I believe, would restrict the room for schooners in the harbour at St. John's is not valid. Under this plan there would be room for schooners to berth instead of anchor and there would be the ideal harbour where every vessel could tie up and have access to the shore instead of anchoring in midstream. I hope the government will find it possible to go ahead without delay with the harbour work. It will not only facilitate trade but should mean lower handling costs and, finally, lower costs to consumers.
There is something else I should like to mention with regard to St. John's or, for that matter, any suitable port. That is the construction of a grain elevator with a flour mill. St. John's or any other suitable port in that general area would be ideally situated for the distribution of feed grains as well as flour. I would say that roughly a million people could be served by a flour mill in St. John's. Not only the maritimes but the West Indies and South America and Europe also could be supplied from the Newfoundland port during the winter when the St. Lawrence is closed to navigation.
Far from hurting Nova Scotia it should promote and improve trade between Halifax and St. John's because it would provide return trade. Two-way trade would bring down freight rates generally and should stimulate trade between the maritime provinces and Newfoundland. The result would be that all the Atlantic provinces would benefit. One point often overlooked particularly when looking at a flat map but which is easily understandable when looking at a globe is that the
8, 1958
National Development Policy port of St. John's is nearer to South America by several hundred miles, I believe, than is the port of New York.
I mentioned air strips a minute ago and I should like to come back to the matter of air services in Newfoundland. Air services in a province such as ours are much more important than in some of the other provinces of Canada. Quite frequently the only reasonably fast communication is by air. Eastern Provincial Airways, the local air line, has done a magnificent job in providing a triangular service in Newfoundland as well as service right down the whole coast of Labrador. The stories of their many mercy flights are legion. Suffice it to say that they have rendered a service unequalled and have brought much needed amenities to the people they serve which heretofore they had to do without. Their big handicap is that during the seasons of freeze-up and break-up it is impossible to operate on either floats or skis. Therefore their service is restricted with considerable discomfort to the public. What is indicated is either the building of air-strips or, what is probably more feasible, the provision of helicopter service during the periods I have mentioned.
Some of the projects I have named are of considerable magnitude and will be costly but I am sure that in a world which is actively considering colonizing the moon it is not too much to ask that development take place within our own realm.
Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, yesterday I listened with great interest to the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and also to the wording of the amendment. You know, it is strange what great changes come over one when he moves across the floor of the house.
We have noticed that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I suppose that works both ways.
It certainly does.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But here we were yesterday listening to the leader of the Liberal party moving by way of an amendment what he described as a national development policy. My thoughts went back to the amendments we moved on several occasions when we were in opposition urging the government of that time to adopt a national policy. We thought we had a patent on national development policy. Therefore it is quite a shock to find the Liberals of all people now coming forward and making a great outcry in support of a national development policy.

Our provocation is greater than yours was when you were on this side.

National Development Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am interested to see how the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) turns himself into a chameleon when he speaks on this amendment.
Oh, I have no intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Our proposals for a national development policy, of course, were a great deal more-
Nebulous.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-Canadian, vigorous and beneficial to the country than this milk and water amendment brought in by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday. I have here a copy of a real national development policy amendment which we moved about a year and a half ago on February 11, 1957. It was in these words:
-that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources, and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.
That amendment, Mr. Speaker, represented the thinking of the Conservative party when in opposition. It represents our thinking today and it emphasizes what we have been trying to do as a government during the last 12 months. It also points to the path that we shall be following in the years that lie ahead. We really do not need any amendment such as that proposed by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday to help us on the way. I refer members to this strange amendment which reads:
This house is of the opinion that, in present circumstances of declining private investment, a balanced policy of national development-
Just what he means by "a balanced policy" nobody knows, unless it was intended to appeal to different parts of the country in the way in which those different parts would prefer to interpret it.
-requires consideration by the government of active measures to meet the urgent needs of social capital-
We did not get a definition of that. I believe this is a favourite expression of Professor Lamontagne-
And also of the minister of northern affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-economic adviser to the
Liberal party at the present time. The use of these words makes me wonder whether or not he wrote the speech the Leader of the Opposition gave yesterday. Here we have:
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
-the urgent needs of social capital especially in the form of transportation facilities, municipal improvements, and other facilities to stimulate economic development and to promote social wellbeing in the settled areas of Canada.
Perhaps it was Knowles who wrote the speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I never thought of that. It is now suggested that perhaps Mr. Stanley Knowles wrote the speech. He may have had something to do with it, but I believe he would have written a much better one if he had had anything to do with the drafting. This reference to social capital had one strange effect which perhaps hon. members might have noticed. It was just like a great big piece of bait on a fish hook for the C.C.F. group and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) rose to the bait and swallowed it, hook, line and sinker, without batting an eyelash.
Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
I wonder if he would care to say how many times his own Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) referred to this term "social capital" in his budget address?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not keep track of how many times my colleagues refer to social capital. They may have caught this bad idea from the other side of the house. In any event, it would be extremely helpful to have a definition of just what social capital means. If it means the same thing to the Leader of the Opposition as it means to the members of the C.C.F., then we are witnessing quite a change across the floor of the House of Commons. We may be witnessing the first exciting hours of a courtship between these two forlorn opposition parties.
However, I would point out to the Leader of the Opposition and his social capitalists that he had better be careful about getting too friendly with these people over in the corner.
That is what got you into office, was it not, under the leadership of Stanley Knowles?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am afraid the Liberal party is never going to get into office on an amendment such as the one it moved yesterday. I have here a statement of just what this group in the corner stand for, and what they mean when they talk about social capital. The heading is "Capitalism still target of C.C.F.". The article is from the Vancouver Province of June 2, 1958. At that time, at their provincial meeting, they passed the following resolution:
The C.C.F. will not rest content until capitalism has been eradicated and the lull program of socialistic planning has been instituted.

I am rising on a point of order. The leader opposite has been very eloquent on subjects which are not germane to the amendment before the house, and certainly an academic discussion of socialism could, by no stretch of even the ingenious imagination of the leader opposite, be considered to be germane.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I was commenting on the fact that these two opposition parties rushed into each other's arms so quickly yesterday when this amendment was put forward. I am simply trying to warn Liberals of the great danger of this courtship. In so far as the member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is concerned, he has said some peculiar things at times, Mr. Speaker. I have here a statement he made on April 15, 1956, which is headed "Liberals victory good for mankind, Pickersgill says":
Immigration Minister Pickersgill said Saturday-
Speaking to the Young Liberals in Toronto.
-"It is not merely for the well-being of Canadians but for the good of mankind in general that the present Liberal government should remain in office."
This illustrates the lack of judgment and what a false prophet the hon. member really is. Mankind seems to be doing much better now than it was two years ago under the government of which he was a member.
Whom do you think you are kidding?
It has been good for 22 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have something that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said, too. Two years ago these ex-ministers were riding very high. Speaking to some Liberals in Vancouver-they are hard to find now, but at that time there were quite a few- the hon. member said:
The smiling minister told a rally in Mount Pleasant memorial hall the Conservative party is "already bankrupt". He foresaw little opposition to the Liberals in the next national election.
"There is no Conservative party today", he said.

Since the minister is in a good mood, I may tell him I was seeking to say that the Conservative party, under men like Borden and Bennett, had disappeared and the Conservative party, in its effort to get into power, had simply adopted Liberal policies and, I might say, quite cleverly Liberal tactics.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member, naturally, is very clever, but this alibi two years later does not ring true at all.
In any event, here we are considering this very pale imitation of a national development policy amendment. I do not believe that very many people across the country,
National Development Policy or even across the floor of this house, are going to take it very seriously. There has been a good deal of discussion about whether the government has done this or has done that to bring about the development of the country. Naturally, there are differences of opinion. We believe that a great deal has been done in the few months we have been in office. Certainly, no one ever tried harder to get things done, and I think that is true of the officials in the departments. I doubt if there has ever been a time in Canadian history when a more honest, genuine and sincere attempt has been made to further developments of every kind across the nation.
In spite of the weeping and wailing we hear from across the way, there has been quite a bit of comment. We have heard from various members of the opposition that all these works projects were a myth, that they will not be undertaken for months or perhaps for years and that there is nothing to be seen of them across the country and nobody is being put to work. I have here a dispatch of June 20 from the "Daily Commercial News and Building Record" dealing with the construction that is actually going on in Canada:
Canada's 51 builders' exchanges in the near future probably will be more active than ever due to a shot in the arm in the shape of current predictions that the nation's construction program for 1958 will total a record $7,136 million. The official prediction makes the 1958 total top last year's $7,048 million by 1.3 per cent.
Surely, in all fairness, Canada having a record year in the construction industry in 1958, the government is entitled to some credit for that result. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that the actions of the government have played a large part in that result. Then in yesterday's Gazette, under the heading "Canadian Construction Record Set as 20 p.c. Gain Reported", we find the following:
Canada's construction industry is continuing to set records. The total cumulative dollar volume of contract awards for the first half of 1958 is the largest ever listed.
This is in a time when business is not as good as it had been, a time when we are in recession. Yet we find the construction industry this year doing more than it has ever done before in the history of Canada. The article continues:
Statistics compiled from Hugh C. MacLean Building Reports show that the 1958 six-month total of construction contract awards is $1,683,261,700, 20 per cent higher than it was at the end of this period last year, and four per cent higher than it was in 1956, the previous record year for the first six months' total.
So much for construction generally. We are very proud of those figures and I think we
2022	HOUSE OF
National Development Policy have good reason to be proud of them. We hope they will be even better as 1958 goes on.
Then I wish to say a few words about one branch of the construction industry, and incidentally I may say it is a branch in which there has been the greatest increase since this government took office. I refer to the house building branch. Here I suppose we have an example of social capital. I presume that the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) would agree that money advanced by the government for purposes of house building would be included in this mysterious classification of social capital.
As hon. members know,-and I do not intend to repeat at any length today-the government decided last August to initiate a small home loan policy. That policy has been extremely successful. The figures for loans under this policy, up to the time when we practically ran out of money in May, are $255,009,800 for a total of 26,030 units. This money would not have been spent had the government not adopted the policy we did adopt for small home loans.
You cannot say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I can say that. Practically none of it would have been spent had it not been for the policy adopted by this government.
You have not shown that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Moneys were being spent for other types of housing but this was a brand new policy devised by a brand new government which was a great improvement on the old government.
Would the minister permit a question?
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has unlimited time.

Was this policy not
embodied in the statute which the minister found on the statute books?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This policy was embalmed by the former government in the statute books and that is exactly where it would have been if the former government had continued in office.
There are certain features about this small home loan plan which deserve comment before I go on to show what has happened since May. In comparing the average income of the person who benefitted under the small home loan plan with that of the home owner taking out an ordinary insured loan, we find that under the small home loan plan the average income is $4,986 whereas the income of the average person getting a loan


under the insured provision is $5,997, over $1,000 a year higher. The average cost of this small home is $12,905 compared with $15,337 for the person getting a loan under the ordinary N.H.A. provisions. These comparisons are for the first quarter of 1958. The average loan under the small home loan plan was $10,706 and under the N.H.A. ordinary provisions it was $11,609. The average down payment-and here is the greatest difference-under the small home loan plan in the first three months of this year was $2,199 and under the insured plan under the ordinary N.H.A. provision it was $3,728, a difference of over $1,500.
As hon. members know we came to the house in May, shortly after this session commenced, and asked for additional funds. We were given another $350 million. Since May 22, which was approximately when the funds first became available-and mind you, there was roughly $10 million remaining of the old fund-to July 4, which is a period of six weeks, money has been lent for cleaning up the small home plan as it formerly was- that is the money being lent out with the lending institutions and banks acting as agents-to an amount of $23,328,451 for a total of 1961 units. This is within the last six weeks.
Does that mean that only $13 million of the new $350 million that parliament approved has been used? The minister said $10 million was carried over.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, approximately $23,300,000 has been put out in order to wind up the old agency loan plan. In addition to that, $16,177,299 has been put out under our new residual plan which could really be divided into three parts: First, that part for cities and towns with populations of under 55,000, for which part the figure is $6,114,309; then for home owners in cities of over 55,000 population, the figure is $1,615,414; for builders both in cities of over 55,000 and centres under that figure-mind you, in the case of those builders the loans can only be made on small homes-the total is $8,447,576. That means a: total of residual loans under our revised plan since May 22 of $16,177,299.
There is a third category under the limited dividend corporation plan which, as hon. members know, provides rental accommodation for the lower income groups, under which $10,816,738 has been put out. Those figures, to provide for the winding up of the agency loan plan, the new residual plan and the limited dividend plan, give a total of $50,322,488 since May 22, 1958.
Is it correct, then, that $40 million was used out of this figure of $350 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. That amounts to something around $40 million already used of the $350 million voted by this house in May.
We have tried, as a result of the debate which took place in this house when we were getting this additional money, to make the new residual loans available to a far greater extent in the smaller centres. With that objective in mind officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have written to the mayor or the reeve of every centre of over 1,500 people in this country pointing out that this plan is available for the Canadians who live in those smaller centres, forwarding leaflets to them and offering to have officials visit those centres to speak to meetings or to advise city or town councils and render whatever assistance is possible. This, I believe, is having the desired effect, and it now looks as though we will be doing a great deal more lending in the small centres across the country.
In addition, steps have been taken to popularize the smaller home. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation participated in the construction of two sample cheaper homes, and we are hoping that there will be a move towards the building of such homes which will bring the benefit of our housing policy within the reach of a group of Canadians with much smaller incomes than those receiving loans at the present time.
Would the minister permit a question on this point. Is it the intention that these lower cost or lower quality homes will be made available throughout the country or only in rural areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are hoping they will be adopted in all parts of Canada, in the smaller centres as well as in the rural areas.
The minister will recognize that they will not always be acceptable.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If they are not acceptable we cannot do much about it.
In many of the urban areas they will not meet the required standards.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
If they are not acceptable what we can do is very limited.
Another very encouraging sign is that in the Atlantic provinces there has been a great increase in the number of requests for loans. We were worried last year because these small home loans were not being taken up in the Atlantic provinces in as large proportions as in other parts of Canada. In the first 25 weeks of 1958, 880 applications for loans of all kinds were received from the Atlantic provinces, in which the National
National Development Policy Housing Act was involved, as compared with 357 applications last year. This is an increase of 146.5 per cent, and we are very much encouraged by this improvement.
Housing starts have shot up. You know, you would not think there was any recession within 10,000 miles of Canada when you consider the housing picture. Housing starts in urban centres during the first half of 1958 were 66 per cent higher than in the corresponding period in 1957. A similar increase is estimated for the rural areas and the prospect for the year as a whole is for starts in excess of 140,000 units.
We were worried as to whether these small homes would sell, and whether as a result of this policy we might find a lot of homes would be unsold across the country. Sales have been good despite a higher level of completions this year, and the inventory of unoccupied houses has declined. At the end of May there were 2,144 dwellings unoccupied for one month or more. A year ago in that category there were 2,662 dwellings.
This all goes to show that the policies of this government have been wise and that the country is not enveloped in a great black cloud as one would gather from listening to the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition and some of his colleagues across the way.
Look at the level of unemployment and you will see.

The Canadian construction
association, which is a non-partisan organization and a splendid one, has this to say:
1957 was a difficult year for the housebuilding section of the construction industry and demonstrated the very considerable way in which the level of residential construction is dependent upon government policy. Had it not been for the timely and vigorous approach to the problem of a shortage of private mortgage funds by the government in August, it is apparent that the volume of house building and employment would have been much lower during the fall and winter months. Like most years, 1957 was affected by a number of conflicting influences in the housing field; some good and some bad. On balance, the favourable factors had won out by the end of the year. Completions rose to over 117,000 compared with a predicted total of 100,000, and the large number of housing starts in the second half of the year and a predicted decrease in competing demands for investment funds gave promise of an increased housing program in 1958.
I forgot to mention that the ordinary loans under the National Housing Act have also been greatly increased this year. Ordinary

National Development Policy National Housing Act loans for the first twenty-seven weeks of last year numbered 13,002 and for the first twenty-seven weeks of this year they numbered 25,121, almost double last year's total.
I have outlined the attempts the government has made to implement a national development policy so far as construction is concerned and particularly housebuilding which is the biggest industry in Canada in these modern times. The government has taken the same approach in every other field of governmental activity including northern affairs, transport and defence production. The same approach was taken in all the activities that were undertaken by the government.
I plead with the Leader of the Opposition not to be so downhearted and pessimistic about Canada. It is terrible to see one with such a lighthearted, genial and cheery character trying to shed crocodile tears all over the House of Commons. It is not fitting. It is not in character at all for him to be acting like that.

Ottawa's explanation for the Canadian pickup: The Canadian government has gone in vigorously for pump priming. This has spurred housing, kept consumer spending and farm incomes high, boosted capital expenditures as well.

Mr. Speaker, before launching my brief contribution to this debate I should like to make reference to a few points that were raised by hon. gentlemen opposite and particularly by those members of the cabinet who spoke. -and all the little echoes and all the little parts of Canada where all the little minds come from answered in tune.
That is a classic example of the arrogance and insult that northern Ontario will not tolerate. That may be in large part the reason why no hon. members on the government side of the house represent ridings in northern Ontario. Northern Ontario may not have caught the vision expounded upon by the minister yesterday for a very valid reason. Perhaps the people in that part of the country have had a sorry experience in the past with visions similar to that outlined by the minister. They have seen a government open up a part of the country and turn it over to what government members like to describe as free enterprise. They have seen fortunes and resources cleared out of those areas leaving in their wake the wrecks of human lives which were employed and exploited in those areas and the fortunes and profits amassed there by so-called free enterprisers have gone to build up other parts of the country.
I recall the remarks of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the committee on mines, forests and waters when he pointed out the mistakes that had been made in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do not believe the hon. member is entitled to discuss the evidence heard in a committee of this house until such time as the committee has completed its investigation and reported back to the house.

Sit down, junior.

Mr. Speaker, let us put it this way. The errors made in the United States in the last 50 years and the way in which they have squandered their natural resources are common knowledge. It is to be hoped that this program of northern development will not be a repetition of what has happened in the United States. Let us hope that this government will have the foresight and the vision, if you want to call it that, to ensure that the same thing does not happen in this country; that we do not squander our wonderful wealth of natural resources as the United States has done.
There is one other small aspect of this northern development which was drawn to my attention just last weekend. I was talking to a gentleman from the Timmins riding who is a silicosis pensioner, living on a pension of roughly $102 a month. He happens to live quite close to the crossroads where highway 11 branches off highway 101 going north through Cochrane and Kapuskasing and the trans-Canada highway. As a result of the position of his home his house is the first place hit by the unemployed from southern Ontario and other parts of Canada who, hoping and trusting in this vision, may think there is some employment for them in the northern part of the country. When they hitch-hike a ride to this crossroads they get off to look for further lifts up the highway and they generally stop in at this old gentleman's place to try to get a cup of coffee or something to eat. He took the trouble last weekend to count the people who stopped at his house asking for something to eat and the number totalled 47. With his pension he does not have too much to feed himself and his family but fortunately, contrary to the present decision of the government which has refused to extend any unemployment insurance benefits to the people whose benefits have run out, at least he never turned them away. He gave them a sandwich before they went on their way.
He must have been a Conservative.

He happens to be a paid up member of the C.C.F. and has been for years.
We also had an interesting example yesterday of an interjection from the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) who seems to be carrying on a contest with the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) as to

National Development Policy which one of them can drag up the old chestnut of the box factory in Saskatchewan.
I must say that they make me a little bit homesick. . They remind me so much of my mother-in-law's parrot. He is 31 years of age and he knows only one question, but he repeats it very often, very loud and very clear. It is not interested in getting an answer, just in asking the question.
We also had an example last night of the amazement demonstrated by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees). I turn to page 1996 of Hansard, where I find the following:
Then we see the C.C.F. climbing aboard the free enterprise bandwagon. Now they are grasping to their breasts small business as though they had always been brothers.
It is rather strange to see this amazement on the part of the minister because I know he was in the house at the very time that this matter was debated by Mr. Owen Jones, the former C.C.F. member for Okanagan Boundary, and also by Mr. Fred Zaplitny, the former member for Dauphin. If hon. members will take the trouble to look up page 3502 of Hansard of April 12, 1957, and page 3448 of April 11, 1957, they will see that members of this group very clearly expounded the case for the small businessman of this country.
I would also like to remind the minister that the amazement which he expressed yesterday was expressed better, I might say, by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), I think it was, as his contribution to the debate on that day. It seems so strange but hon. members know, or at least should know, that the very backbone of the C.C.F. party has been the small businessman across the country.
Then, of course, we had the reference by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) today. Like the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker), he took great glee in referring to some decision made by the C.C.F. party of British Columbia. I find it very strange that their memories do not go back to a recent decision made by the Progressive Conservative party of British Columbia which apparently did not sit too well with the rest of the Progressive Conservatives across the country.
I was very pleased to hear the minister speak of the tremendous improvement in housing in this country. I would like to suggest, that possibly the same treatment might be handed out to small business that was given to the housing industry in this country. If the government could see its way to extend the same assistance to the small businesses in this country that they have given to housing, then we might see the same beneficial results accruing therefrom.

Contrary to what hon. members may believe and certainly contrary to what they state across this country, the C.C.F. party has never been against free enterprise.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

The hon. member is asking for something, and as a matter of fact we had the question yesterday. What is the percentage of small business that requires the help the hon. member is speaking about? If the government does not know the percentage how can the help be given?
The retail merchants association says almost all of them.
To what did the hon. member refer?
The retail merchants association.
What authority has the hon. member for saying that?
I will quote it to the house the next day the subject is discussed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry; we cannot have a debate of this kind. The hon. member who has the floor may continue.

I recall hon. members on the government side appearing to be quite interested in questioning each and every one of this group who rises in his place as to what is his particular definition of a certain thing. I would suggest they look up the debate of April 11 and 12 of last year, which I mentioned before, where I think they will find much of the information and data they are requesting at the present time. I could have put it on Hansard again but there are other members who wish to speak in this debate and I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house than is necessary. Certainly, today the small businessmen in the country are in a very serious condition. They are being squeezed out right and left by huge corporations which are sprawling across the country. The point might be made that these large corporations may be more efficient, and I will not deny it. But I do not believe that efficiency and efficiency only should be the sole yardstick in this matter. I think the personal service of the small storekeeper, the small shop, is something that we should make every effort to hang onto in this country.
As I mentioned before, contrary to what is preached about this group, we are not against free enterprise as free enterprise. We are, and always have been and will continue to be, against monopoly enterprise which chokes the very life out of free enterprise.

Apparently, hon. members on the government side are unable to differentiate between the two.
I could go into further detail on this matter, Mr. Speaker, but I will merely refer to a chart prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics showing the percentage of increase or decrease in respect of independents and corporate chains in this country. For Canada as a whole I find that from 1951 to 1956 corporate chains increased from 35 per cent to 41 per cent and as a result independents decreased from 65 per cent to 59 per cent. I find that in my own province of Ontario the rate of change is even faster. In that same period from 1951 to 1956 corporate chains increased from 49 per cent to 56 per cent and as a result the independents were reduced from 51 per cent to 44 per cent.
I say it is high time that the government of the country should look into the matter and provide some form of assistance to the small businessman who really is the true, free enterpriser. The government should make sure that some effort is made to give small businessmen a hand before they become extinct.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words to point out some of the contradictions and confusion that certainly exist in the minds of some of the members of the C.C.F. group. We have before the house an amendment to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). He wishes to add certain words to the motion of nonconfidence of the Liberal opposition, those words being "long term loans to qualifying small businesses".
When the hon. member for Kootenay West first got up he congratulated the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for his efforts, as he put it, to rescue this country from the deficiencies of private enterprise. He even went so far as to state that he would issue a membership ticket to the Leader of the Opposition. He had no sooner finished that statement than he started to expound how the amendment put forward by his party could save that same private enterprise about which he was talking.
There is also a considerable amount of confusion in the minds of the members of the C.C.F. party as to what may constitute a qualifying small business. The hon. member for Kootenay West stated that it was a business primarily interested in the local community. He also said it was a business that did not call on foreign or exterior capital and also was a business that would reinvest all its profits in the locality. In answer to a question at the end of his speech he said that a small business was a business that 57071-3-128J
National Development Policy could not issue shares or float loans by means of debentures or bonds.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am not an exponent or particular friend of big business but I do know that big business as it exists and is organized today is certainly most vitally interested in the community in which it engages in its activities. As everyone knows, when a business locates in a particular place it employs local labour. Every effort is always made to find among the local population all the help that the industry needs. It is also the employees of so-called big business, which in the minds of the C.C.F. members represents such a menace to this country who are most active in all social welfare activities. You see them as heads and directors of social clubs. You see them everywhere taking the interests of the community to heart. Certainly they are the first contributors to all public campaigns where contributions are necessary to help worthy causes in the particular area.
If so-called big business has had to call on foreign capital it is because such capital was not available where the resource was being developed, the mill was established or the plant or industry happened to be. It is because capital could not be found locally that they have applied for and in certain cases obtained capital from exterior sources. There is absolutely nothing wrong about such a procedure.
The hon. member went further and said that the profits of small businesses are reinvested locally. That may or may not be so. In many cases the owners of so-called small businesses do not even live where the profits are made. These businesses, although small, may be controlled from a distance and the profits that the owners make may certainly be reinvested elsewhere, even outside the country. Therefore that is not a true definition of what a qualifying small business may be.
Nor is the definition any more accurate when the hon. member states that it is a business that cannot issue shares or raise loans by debentures or bonds. As we know, many small businesses today are incorporated. The shares may belong wholly only to one, two or three persons. Yet these incorporated businesses can issue shares and raise money by bonds while at the same time remaining small businesses. That was one definition given to us as to what constitutes a small business.
The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) gave another definition in answer to a question. He said that in the United States a small business is one that has a turnover of less than $5 million. He went on to say that in Canada it might be only
